title: Jerusalem, 1187
hookLine: Salah al-Din retakes Jerusalem and lets many ransom out or leave in peace

lines: WHAT ABOUT THOSE WHO CAN'T PAY?
cards: The city has surrendered. Inside the walls, families are counting coins on kitchen tables.

The terms, as the sultan's own secretary records them, are plain: each person may pay a ransom, take their goods and walk out of the gate within a set time. Some can pay. Some can't, and they know it.

At the gate, the clerks sit with their lists, and everyone waits to see what the winner will do about the people with nothing to hand over. The winner is Salah al-Din, and the city is the one Arabic calls the holy.

teach.b: In Arabic, Jerusalem is usually al-Quds, the holy.

It's the city of the Aqsa mosque, linked with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his night journey, and the hadith collections report that the believers once faced toward it in prayer, before the qiblah turned to Mecca.
The Crusaders had held it, and Muslim chroniclers remembered the day they took it as a day of killing. So payback might have been expected. What the accounts describe instead is a surrender on terms.
Imad al-Din, the sultan's secretary, who was there, writes of the ransom and the gate. Then the part beyond the terms.
The sultan's brother, al-Adil, the accounts say, asked for a group of the poor as a gift, and set them free. Salah al-Din released others himself, among them the old, and let widows go.
They also say that those who could not pay and were not freed were taken captive. Mercy came, and it didn't reach everyone. It was a choice made at a gate, by people, imperfectly.

teach.h: PARDON IS BETTER, THE QUR'AN SAYS.
teach.b: The story sits close to a teaching in the Qur'an. In surah an-Nahl, if the believers punish, the punishment must match the wrong done to them, no more; and if they bear it patiently, that is better.
Surah ash-Shura makes the same turn: an injury may be answered with its like, but whoever pardons and makes peace, their reward is with Allah. The Qur'an allows a fair answer. It praises the pardon.
Winning is when that costs most, because winning is when you could.

how: Muslims retell Salah al-Din's taking of Jerusalem in sermons, books and classrooms, and the release of people who could not pay the ransom is often told as an example of mercy in victory.

o: the city Muslims face in prayer today
a fortress town on the coast of Syria
al-Quds, the holy city of the Aqsa mosque

p: a price to go free and leave
asked for a group of the poor, freed them
the sultan's secretary, who wrote it down

s: the accounts say those who couldn't pay and weren't released were taken captive. mercy came, but not to all.
the accounts say some who could not pay were freed anyway
al-Adil freed a group of the poor, and Salah al-Din released others, among them the old.
the Qur'an forbids any answer to a wrong
it allows an answer that matches the wrong, and says bearing it patiently, or pardoning, is better.

games.q: you're Salah al-Din. Jerusalem has surrendered, the ransom is set, and crowds of poor people can't pay it. what do you do?
o: hold to the terms, exactly as written.
let some of those who can't pay go free.
punish the city for what was done in it before.
games.why: the accounts say his brother al-Adil freed a group of the poor and the sultan released others himself. not everyone went free, and the chroniclers say so.

practice: Bring to mind somewhere you're ahead right now: an argument you won, a sibling who owes you an apology. Notice the pull to press it, then choose one small mercy, like letting the point drop or leaving the final message unsent.
If you pray, ask Allah for a soft heart in the moment you could be hard; if not, hold that person in mind with some kindness.

wordCard.voice: Jerusalem. In Arabic, al-Quds, the holy. The city Salah al-Din took back, where a ransom was set at the gate and some who couldn't pay walked out free. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the holy, a name for Jerusalem, from the root q-d-s, holiness.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy in victory. A fair answer is allowed; the pardon is praised. That's plenty for today.
